class.name: RockGenerator
class.brief_description: Makes rocks and stones as real geometry: broken along the joints of a rock type, rounded by transport, weathered.
class.description: Each rock is a block cut by the joint planes of its rock type (near-cuboid, as natural fragments are: Domokos et al. 2020), with secondary fractures, impact chips and partial cracks, held as a signed distance field. Transport rounds it by Bloore's abrasion flow (the surface moves in at [code]1 + c * curvature[/code]: corners first, then slow shrinking; Domokos et al. 2014), for [member transport_distance] metres of river against the rock type's abrasion length. Weathering by rock type is carved in: spheroidal rounding of granite and basalt, solution pits on limestone tops, sandstone laminae and tafoni, basalt vesicles, slate cleavage steps, glacial striations. Surface nets make the mesh, meshoptimizer its LODs. The mesh rests on its flattest side (local Y the short axis, X the long one) and its b axis is 2 units long. See docs/ideas/rocks.md.

method.name: generate
method.description: Makes one rock for the current [member seed]. Its metadata: [code]rock_axes[/code] (half lengths along x, y, z: long, short and intermediate axis), [code]rock_bottom[/code] (lowest y), [code]rock_hull[/code] (up to 48 points for a convex collision shape), [code]rock_faces[/code] (the planes it broke along), [code]rock_roundness[/code], [code skip-lint]rock_type[/code] and [code]rock_family[/code]. The mesh rests on its flattest side and its b axis is 2 units long, so an instance scaled by [code]s[/code] is a stone of b-axis diameter [code]2 s[/code].

method.name: generate_library
method.description: Makes [param count] rocks from seeds [member seed] to [code]seed + count - 1[/code] on worker threads.

method.name: get_effective_salt
method.description: The salt in use: [member salt], or the family's own when that is below 0 (1 for sea stacks, arches and platforms, 0.4 for cave mouths, 0 inland).

method.name: get_last_build_msec
method.description: Milliseconds the last [method generate] or [method generate_library] took.

method.name: get_last_triangle_count
method.description: Triangles in the most detailed level of the last rock, or of all rocks of the last library.

method.name: get_material
method.description: The shared material of a rock type: mineral colour and specks, bands, weathered rind, lichen and moss, a ground contact band, the water film, the weather wetness (drying patchily, tops and sunny sides first) with rivulets down the steep faces while it rains ([code]rain_rivulets[/code], from the flow routing baked into the vertex colour alpha), and snow.

method.name: get_roundness
method.description: Roundness reached by [member transport_distance] for this rock type, from 0 (fresh) to 1 (fully rounded), from the rock type's abrasion length.

method.name: get_shader_code
method.description: The source of the rock shader used by [method get_material].

members.member: Build the close-up version of the shape: the same stone on a grid of about 3 mm cells at the family's typical size (at most 300 cells across), with the rock's millimetre fabric carved in as geometry. Several times the triangles; meant for stones within a few metres of the camera (see [member RockField3D.close_up_radius]).
Scales the grid resolution of the shape. Lower is faster and coarser.

What made the rock: fresh rockfall, scree, glacial boulder, river cobble, beach pebble or cliff block. Sets the size of the block, how much it is chipped, rounded and flattened, and the default resolution.

When above 1, the stone is also split into about this many pieces for breaking, stored in the mesh metadata: [code]rock_chunks[/code] holds one [Mesh] arrays [Array] per piece in the stone's frame, [code]rock_bonds[/code] holds [Dictionary]s ([code]chunks[/code], [code]centroid[/code], [code]normal[/code], [code]area[/code]), and there are also [code]rock_chunk_volumes[/code] and [code]rock_volume[/code]. The cells are a Voronoi split taken in domain-warped space, stretched across the bedding of sandstone, limestone and slate, so the walls are rough breaks and layered rock splits into slabs. Each piece keeps the stone's own surface and marks; its new faces are fresh breaks. Slivers are merged into their neighbours. See [method RockField3D.break_stone].
Builds distance levels of detail for the mesh.

The size, in metres per unit, that the close-up marks (crystals, laminae, striae) and a fracture's break relief are carved at, snapped to whole octaves from the family's typical size. The shader lays out its mineral colours at the same step from each stone's real size, so relief and colour share one map and crystals stay within 41% of their real size. 0 uses the family's typical size. [RockField3D] sets it per close-up and fracture shape.
Grid cells across the rock. [code]0[/code] uses the family's own resolution.
The rock: how it is jointed and breaks, how fast it abrades, how it weathers and its colour.

Sea-spray salt, 0 to 1: how strongly salt weathering hollows the stone. Sandstone, granite and limestone get tafoni, cavernous hollows a tenth to a third of the stone across with a hood over each opening and smaller hollows nested inside, and honeycomb cells about 6 cm across with thin walls over their sides. Old inland blocks (tors, hoodoos, goblins, fins, and any well-weathered stone) get them too, fewer and smaller. Below 0: the family's own (see [method get_effective_salt]).
Seed of the rock. Each seed gives a different rock of the same type and family.
Collapses edges of the most detailed level only where neither the surface nor its normal moves visibly, which keeps every chip, pit and groove with fewer triangles.
Metres the rock travelled before it came to rest, which rounds it by Bloore abrasion: corners first, then slow shrinking. Below 0 uses the family's own distance.
Strength of weathering in place, from 0 to 1: spheroidal rounding, solution pits, laminae, tafoni. Below 0 uses the family's own.

constants.constant: Massive crystalline rock: few joints, spheroidal weathering, grey with dark and light specks.
Bedded, pale, with solution pits.
Bedded and laminated, warm, wears fastest, with tafoni hollows.
Dark, in five to seven-sided columns, with vesicles.
Dark grey, splits in thin cleavage plates.
Number of rock types.
Fresh blocks fallen from a cliff.
Smaller fresh stones on talus, chipped on the way down.
Subrounded boulders out of till, with a striated facet.
River stones rounded by [member transport_distance].
Beach stones, rounded and flattened by the swash.
Large jointed blocks set into cliff faces.
Tor blocks: joint blocks rounded in place by deep weathering (woolsack edges, flat sheeting faces), most with a weathering pan on top.

A sea stack: one jointed column of bedrock (its x axis up once stood on end), banded by harder and softer beds, notched about a fifth of the way up where the sea works its foot, with open vertical joints from the top.
A sea arch: a bedded wall of bedrock (x the span, y up) with the opening the waves cut through it from the bed up through most of its height.
A wave-cut platform: a thin bench of bedrock (x along the shore, z out to sea) with two joint sets opened into grooves, low ledges stepping down seaward and a few rock pools.
A hoodoo: a column of soft bedded rock (x up when stood on end), beaded by its softer beds and narrowing to a neck under a wider, harder caprock.
Limestone pavement: a flat slab of bedrock dissolved along two joint sets into clints between deep, narrow grykes, with solution pans on the tops.

A sandstone fin: a narrow wall of bedrock between two joints (x along it, z up), its top and ends rounded, an alcove at a weak bed near the foot and, in about half of them, an arch through it with a smooth, catenary-like head.

A slab of river bedrock (x down the flow) drilled with round, undercut potholes in a line, some breached into each other, the bed polished and fluted. The mesh meta [code]rock_potholes[/code] holds each pothole's floor and radius (x, y, z, r in the stone's frame).
A goblin: a sandstone knob 1 to 6 m tall (x up when stood), rounded all over by spheroidal weathering, a bulbous head on a narrower neck over a flared foot.

A cave mouth: a limestone outcrop (x along the cliff, z up, the front face +y) with a passage opening into it along a bed or a joint, its roof bedding-flat or arched, narrowing and turning as it goes in to a blind end.

A ledge slab: the hard caprock bed of a bench standing out over the weaker bed under it (x along the lip, y the bed's thickness, z out over the lip), its lip broken along slanted joints, its soffit's front edge bevelled up, sometimes a stress-release crack open behind the lip.
Number of families.
